https://www.elledecor.com/life-culture/t.text: Somewhere in a shoebox, a filing cabinet, or an aunt's attic, there just might be a document that could open the door to a new citizenship. It could be a grandparent's birth certificate, a great-grandmother's naturalization papers, or an old family surname traced back to Naples or Kraków. Some European countries allow citizenship by descent, or jus sanguinis, meaning nationality can pass through family lines rather than birthplaces. In many cases, that can open the door to EU citizenship rights, including the ability to live, work, and study there. Below are five countries where ancestry may make you eligible. But just a note: the rules vary widely and often depend on what documentation you have—they also may change over time.ItalyIn Italy, citizenship by descent must come through an unbroken line of descent. The applicant must trace their family line back to someone alive after March 17, 1861 (Italian unification), and no one in the chain can have naturalized elsewhere before their child’s birth.An ancestor who naturalized abroad prior to June 14, 1912 cannot pass on citizenship, and there are a few other restrictions that can apply based on the local consulate. Applications go through the Italian consulate of residence, run about 600 euros in fees, and require apostilled, translated vital records for every generation in the chain.IrelandA parent born in Ireland makes you automatically Irish. A grandparent born on the island of Ireland means you can register through the Foreign Births Register (FBR) and become a citizen. However, if the citizen was a great-grandparent, the parent of the applicant must have registered in the FBR before the applicant was born. Registering afterward, even successfully, does not extend citizenship back a generation.Great-grandchildren who missed that window can try the discretionary “Irish associations” route under Section 16 of the 1956 Citizenship Act, but the country grants this rarely, and it requires three years of Irish residency plus proof of cultural or economic ties. FBR registration costs a fee set by the Irish government and currently takes around a year, though processing times can change.PolandIn Poland, there is no fixed generational cap, but eligibility depends on proving an unbroken chain of citizenship and no disqualifying loss of citizenship. A great-great-grandchild of a post-1920 Polish citizen can qualify, as long as no one in the chain formally renounced citizenship along the way. Poland calls this process “Confirmation of Polish Citizenship” rather than an application, because the law treats the applicant as already a citizen by descent.The anchor ancestor has to have held citizenship after 1920, when the modern Polish state reformed after World War I. Someone descended from an ancestor who left partitioned Poland before 1920, when it was still split between Austria-Hungary, Prussia, and Russia, generally cannot transmit citizenship. Confirmation goes through a Polish consulate and typically takes many months or over a year.Germany Germany runs two ancestry routes. The standard jus sanguinis path, under Section 4 of the Nationality Act, requires an unbroken chain of ancestry through a German parent or grandparent who did not naturalize elsewhere before the next generation’s birth.The second path, Article 116(2) of the Basic Law, covers descendants of people stripped of German citizenship by the Nazi regime between 1933 and 1945 for political, racial, or religious reasons. It has no statute of limitations and applies retroactively, covering groups such as children of German mothers and children of unmarried German fathers who were previously excluded from citizenship transmission. Germany allows dual citizenship on both routes, and neither requires language proficiency or residency.HungaryThere is no fixed generational limit and no residency requirement for citizenship, but applicants must pass a Hungarian language interview. The simplified naturalization track requires proof that an ancestor held Hungarian citizenship, documented through birth, marriage, or church records, followed by a basic conversational assessment at a consulate.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckg9.text: Image caption, Images of the damaged vessel have been verified by the BBC By Yolande Knell ,Â Middle East correspondent Â and Â Michael Sheils McNamee Published 11 August 2026, 14:35 BST Updated 3 hours ago Four people have reportedly been killed in an attack on a small cargo ship in the Red Sea suspected to have been carried out by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, the internationally recognised government of Yemen has said. If confirmed, it would be the first deadly strike by the group on a vessel since the US and Israel started a conflict against Iran. Yemen's transport ministry said the ship was hit with three ballistic missiles, south of the port of Mocha, causing a fire on board and resulting in the deaths of four crew - three Pakistanis and one Indonesian. The Houthis began attacks on shipping last month - announcing a naval blockade of Saudi ports. They have not admitted carrying out the attack. The conflict in the region has been ongoing since the end of February, punctuated by a faltering ceasefire which was meant to lead to a deal to end the war. It has whipped up regional tensions, with the Houthis also attacking Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and oil facilities, in parallel with Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz - the vital waterway where a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit. The attack comes after a years-long truce in Yemen's civil war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government collapsed last month. The Houthis control much of north-western Yemen, and frequently clash with the government. The government operates out of Aden in the south, due to the capital Sanaa being held by the Houthis. Social media images examined by BBC Verify appear to show a damaged cargo ship in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which sits at the inlet of the Red Sea, off the coast of Yemen. In its statement, the Yemeni government said the ship had been carrying food, and that the attack on a commercial vessel marked an escalation in approach from the Houthis. In an earlier statement, maritime risk management company Vanguard said the Yemeni Navy deployed to assist the vessel and came under fire. This resulted in three others being injured. Close-up pictures show the vessel is named Tihamah which, according to ship-tracking platform MarineTraffic, is in the Red Sea off Warner Point. Vanguard has identified the ship as sailing under the flag of Tanzania, while shipping website MarineTraffic says it is owned by an Egyptian operator. In its statement, Yemen's ministry of transport referred to Tihama as a "Yemeni commercial ship", while earlier reports in Iranian media referred to it as "Saudi-affiliated". The pictures of the vessel, which were shared by Iran's semi-official Mehr news agency, have been verified as new and show no signs of AI-generation. https://www.warringtonguardian.co.uk/new.text: Nostalgia Warringtons 'quiet soldiers' who walked in the shadow of war By Rod Scotney Share 0 Comments Appleton Hall in Stretton housed POWs (Image: NQ) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. Away from the roar of Warrington’s wartime factories, the regimental pride of the South Lancashire Regiment, and the busy runways of Burtonwood, a quieter history was playing out in the fields of Penketh and the Cheshire plains. Threaded through the marshy lands edging Widnes is a story softer in tone, but no less significant: the history of the prisoner of war camps that shaped local life from 1914 to 1945, and of the men who arrived as enemies but became, for a time, part of Warrington’s working landscape. The First World War: Labour on the Land During the Great War, Warrington did not host a major POW compound within the town centre itself, but it stood inside a web of camps and labour detachments that fed crucial manpower into the region’s struggling farms. Just east of the town, Handforth POW camp became one of the largest internment centres in the North West. Thousands of German soldiers, Austro-Hungarian labourers, and merchant seamen were held behind its wire. From here, working parties were dispatched across Cheshire—including the fringes of Warrington—to tackle acute agricultural shortages. In 1918, a sub-camp opened at Frodsham, sending prisoners directly into the marshes and fields stretching toward Warrington. They dug drainage channels, lifted root crops, and worked land that had been left wanting for hands. For many local farms, these men were quite literally the difference between a failed harvest and a passable one. This connection to POW history also ran in the opposite direction. While enemy prisoners worked the Cheshire soil, Warrington families were busy sending parcels to their own captured soldiers—men of the South Lancashire Regiment held in German camps. Local archives still preserve these records, marking small acts of care that travelled across a broken continent. The Second World War: Camps on the Edge of Town By the 1940s, Warrington’s POW presence was far more visible, with camps, hostels, and working parties becoming part of the district’s daily rhythm. One of the most significant sites was Camp 290, situated on South Lane near Widnes and Penketh. Built on unused Royal Artillery barracks, it initially housed Italian prisoners, who were considered low risk and suitable for agricultural labour. In a remarkable footnote to local history, one of the original wooden huts from Camp 290 was later purchased and used for decades by the 10th Warrington Scouts, giving a wartime barrack an unexpected second life in community service. With so many local men away fighting, Warrington’s farms relied heavily on this captive workforce for the relentless cycles of the agricultural year. Prisoners became a staple of the farming landscape, working alongside local labourers on seasonal planting, drainage maintenance, and the heavy work of lifting potatoes and harvesting sugar beet. Local memories of this era often carry a tone of quiet camaraderie. Prisoners who arrived as enemies became familiar faces in the fields—men who shared jokes, swapped words, and worked under the same rain. German POWs injured during capture or transit also found themselves in the area, occasionally treated at the American military hospitals linked to Burtonwood Airbase and facilities near Appleton. This brought them into direct contact with Allied medical staff and, indirectly, Warrington’s civilian population. Perhaps the most poignant integration happened during the holidays. Local Catholic archives record that Italian and German prisoners from nearby camps were sometimes permitted, under escort, to attend Midnight Mass at St Mary’s RC Church. Even under strict blackout conditions, the church provided a rare moment of shared humanity, with enemy soldiers kneeling quietly among Warrington parishioners, separated by war yet united by ritual. Aftermath and Legacy By 1946, most POWs had been repatriated, though some Italians chose to remain in Britain permanently, marrying locally and settling into post-war life. The physical traces of the camps—the fences, foundations, and timber huts—slowly faded from the landscape. What remains today are fragments: a scout hut built from a camp barrack, a handful of photographs, and the memory of a time when enemy soldiers and Warrington farmers worked side by side in the fields. Warrington’s POW story isn’t one of battles or grand strategy. It’s a story of fields, labour, faith, and fleeting human connections formed in the shadow of war—an understated chapter of local history that still deserves its place in the town’s collective memory. On Monday, the retailer announced a new strategic partnership with Iconic Brands Nordic LLC to bring Gap to more customers across the Nordic and Baltic markets. More from WWD Gap, Malbon Reconnect for Golf-inspired Americana Capsule How Gap x Hailey Bieber Turned '90s Nostalgia Into a Social Media Hit CEO Mark Breitbard on Gap's Formula for Campaigns and the Fall Story Gap 's rollout across the region will take place in three phases, beginning with its launch on Boozt, a Nordic a multi-brand online fashion and lifestyle shop, across Sweden, Denmark, Norway and Finland in August. This will be followed by openings in Stockmann department stores across Finland, Estonia and Latvia. In September, Gap's first dedicated retail store and e-commerce site will launch in Estonia. "Our partnership with Iconic Brands Nordic reflects our long-term commitment to growing Gap in markets where we see meaningful opportunity," said Facundo Ginobili, Gap Inc. senior vice president, franchise and wholesale. "Together, we're bringing the Gap brand to life through storytelling, experiences, partnerships and omnichannel retail, creating modern, relevant ways for customers across the Nordic and Baltic region to discover and engage with the brand." Gap's deal with Iconic Brands Nordic is part of the company's ongoing effort to expand its footprint internationally with the support of companies that possess deep local market knowledge. Earlier this month, the company entered a partnership with Chalhoub Group , the Dubai-based luxury goods retailer and distributor, to bring the Gap, Banana Republic and Athleta brands to the Middle East. In March, Gap Inc. formed a partnership with apparel group Fashionata to lead Gap's distribution and market development in Australia. Iconic Brands Nordic was established in 2025 as a joint venture between Brandgate Group, a a wholesale and retail fashion distributor, and Tristafan, an Estonian investment and holding company. The company's mission is to scale the Gap brand by building a robust retail, wholesale, and digital ecosystem. "We're excited to introduce Gap to even more customers across the Nordic and Baltic markets," said Kristjan Rajando, CEO of Iconic Brands Nordic. "Together with Gap Inc., we're building an omnichannel experience that makes it easier than ever for customers to discover the brand, whether they're shopping online or in store. We believe Gap's iconic style and timeless essentials will resonate strongly across the region." https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/manager-a.text: Berk Uyal Updated Wed, September 9, 2026 at 11:17 AM UTC 0 The case was heard at the Old Bailey -Credit:VV Shots via Getty Images A contracts manager has avoided immediate prison after a labourer was buried alive on a construction site, while two firms have been fined more than £1million over his death. Gheorghita Arsene, 33, who was known as Geo, died when a deep trench collapsed on top of him, covering him in soil as he worked in Banstead, Surrey on June 24 2020. Following a three-month trial at the Old Bailey, principal contractor Appledorn Developments Limited and T Vaughan Limited (TVL) were found guilty of a charge under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974. ‘Planted explosives’ threat at Scottish school as parents keep children at home Body found in hunt for missing boy, 15, who vanished off Wales coast on holiday On Monday, Judge Judy Khan KC fined the now-defunct Appledorn £500,000, saying there had been “cost-cutting at the expense of safety”. T Vaughan Limited (TVL) was fined £650,000 plus £40,000 in costs, with the judge allowing the firm six years to pay. She said the company had systems in place but they had not been sufficiently implemented. Contracts manager Anthony O’Connor, 42, of Romford, Essex , previously pleaded guilty to the same health and safety charge of failing to discharge his duties. He was sentenced to 10 months in custody, suspended for 18 months, and ordered to carry out 150 hours of unpaid work. Judge Judy Khan KC said O’Connor had “actual foresight” of the risk of harm. The accident happened at a site in Park Road where an old care home had been demolished to make way for a new purpose-built care home . The victim had been working to replace a damaged pipe at the bottom of the 10ft deep trench which had been dug with a three-tonne digger. He had been clearing soil with a shovel and pickaxe when without warning the trench walls collapsed. His co-worker on a digger had shouted a warning but Mr Arsene took only a couple of steps before he was covered in earth. His colleague ran for help and desperate attempts were made to get him out and clear away soil from his face and body. Fire and ambulance crews were called to the scene but paramedics’ efforts to revive the Romanian national were hampered by the weight of the soil around him and difficulties in digging him out. As Mr Arsene could not be removed from the trench it was not possible to carry out chest compressions and he was pronounced dead at 2.44pm, an hour after the accident happened. Health and safety inspectors found there were no supports to the trench and the excavated soil had been deposited right next to it, the Old Bailey heard. John McGuinness KC had told jurors: “The prosecution case is that George’s death was entirely avoidable. It should never have happened.” The judge also addressed the circumstances of Mr Arsene’s death as she passed sentence. Judge Khan said: “On the 24 June 2020 Gheorghita Arsene was fatally crushed as he worked on an unsupported deep trench on a construction site. “The loss of his life was a terrible tragedy, particularly as it was totally avoidable.” Previously, a jury deliberated for 73 hours and 28 minutes and was discharged after failing to reach a verdict in relation to a charge of manslaughter against O’Connor. Site manager Peter Wraith, 54, from New Waltham in Lincolnshire , was cleared of manslaughter and assistant site manager Gregory Peake, 51, from Bromley in south-east London, was acquitted of failing to discharge his health and safety duty. Mr Arsene’s mother, Ienuta Arsene, attended the sentencing hearing by videolink from Romania. In a statement, she described her son as a “good man” who sought to support his family. Mitigating for O’Connor, Mark Balysz KC said his client was sorry for the tragedy of Mr Arsene’s death and his role in it. He said: “He clearly regrets the catastrophic mistake he made in allowing the work to continue in relation to the excavation.” O’Connor was TVL’s most senior representative on site on the day of the fatal incident. Mitigating for TVL, Prashant Popat KC said: “This incident has been taken most seriously by TVL. “In the days after the incident TVL and everyone in the company from the top down were deeply troubled and affected by Mr Arsene’s death.” The barrister said the firm, founded by Thomas Vaughan in 2010, retained an ethos of a “small close-knit family-run company” and everything was done “as safely as possible”, with nearly £3million spent on health and safety. He argued TVL’s failings were less than those of Appledorn and that it was an isolated incident. Appledorn, which was not represented in court, went into liquidation in 2023 with assets registered the year before of £2.5million.
